source.title: A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes
source.authors: David A. Klindt; Charles O'Neill; P. Reizinger; Harald Maurer; N. Miolane

record.file_problem: The supplied title differs from the title in the text: the metadata says “A unifying framework from neural superposition to sparse interpretable codes,” while the text is titled “From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks.” The text is otherwise a complete perspective paper.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own tests of additive composition in image-model representations, a related measure of superposition, but does not test the listed versions’ claims about overcomplete sparse features, capacity, LLMs, or feature dimensionality.
record.gate_note: The paper also reviews prior studies and presents theoretical claims about identifiability, compressed sensing, and sparse autoencoders. Those cited results are not rows. Figure 1 reports an additivity comparison against a calibrated baseline and pixel-space comparison; Figure 3 reports a separate analogy cosine similarity.
record.test_reason: A perspective paper. Its only empirical results are illustrative additivity and analogy checks on ViT-B/16 image embeddings (Fig. 1, Fig. 3C). These measure linear composition of representations, not sparse overcomplete feature storage, capacity-driven polysemanticity, SAE recovery or completeness, or feature dimensionality. Its SAE claims (suboptimal recovery, non-universal features) and the Fig. 4 compressed-sensing bounds are theory or cited results (O'Neill et al. 2025; Paulo & Belrose 2025), not results of this paper. The reader's 'tests/T2' overstates the relation; the paper discusses the claim and argues for a linear-superposition framework.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that networks represent features linearly and non-orthogonally (superposition), justified by identifiability theory (Reizinger et al. 2024). They argue that compressed sensing and sparse coding can in principle recover the features up to permutation, with quantitative interpretability metrics as proxies. They note that SAEs recover suboptimally (per their cited O'Neill et al. 2025) and leave open scalable sparse inference, binding, and non-Euclidean or discrete latents.
record.recipe_differences: The original source studies toy networks and superposition geometry; this paper instead gives image-representation additivity examples and a theoretical perspective on identifiability, compressed sensing, and sparse coding.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported additivity result differs between neural representation space (p < 10^-5) and pixel space (p ≈ 0.88).

fits_no_version.finding: Over N=10 image triplets, ViT-B/16 representations of a combined image are significantly closer to the sum of the part representations than a calibrated baseline (p<1e-5). Pixel space shows no such effect (p≈0.88).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Vision-model embeddings compose concepts approximately additively (linear representation), unlike raw pixel space.

fits_no_version.finding: A local pink-elephant analogy in ViT-B/16 gives cosine similarity 0.92.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Image embeddings support vector-arithmetic analogies for attribute–object composition.

record.peer_reviewed: Nature Machine Intelligence (venue stated in supplied metadata); the text identifies itself as arXiv:2503.01824v1.
record.problems: The empirical additivity evidence is limited to image examples and does not test sparse overcomplete feature storage or the listed claim versions. The reported Figure 1 significance values are aggregate; individual cosine values are not provided in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible outcomes identified. Results from prior work summarized in the text were excluded because they are cited findings, not results of this paper.

untested.parts: No toy models, no feature-count vs dimension sweep, no sparsity transition, no geometry.
No test of capacity competition or dedicated vs shared dimensions.
No test of non-capacity causes of polysemanticity.
No measurement of features spread across neurons or of SAE recovery in LLMs. Only cited work and theoretical bounds (Fig. 4).
SAE non-universality and suboptimal recovery are cited (Paulo & Belrose 2025; O'Neill et al. 2025), not tested here.
The non-linear or multi-dimensional features issue is only mentioned in limitations, citing Engels et al. 2024.

record.verdict_notes: The title differs from the metadata (an arXiv v1 of the NMI paper). The 'our results indicate that simple SAEs cannot achieve optimal recovery' sentence refers to the authors' separate cited paper, not to results in this text. Elhage et al. is cited as the source of the non-orthogonality definition.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature-count-to-dimension comparison, sparsity-dependent transition, or regular geometry is tested.
No test of capacity pressure, dedicated dimensions for important features, or feature sharing by neurons.
No test of alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemanticity evidences superposition.
The paper discusses cited LLM and SAE work but does not itself measure feature distribution across neurons or SAE recovery in LLMs.
The paper discusses limitations and non-universality of SAE features based on prior work, but does not itself test their completeness, stability, or canonical status.
No empirical comparison of one-dimensional directions with multidimensional features.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared additivity in neural representation space with a calibrated baseline.

conditions.value: Further examples, N=10; image examples include generated and natural images

rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline (cosine similarity of the representations of A and B)
rows.baseline: Cosine similarity of the representations of just “A” and “B” (calibrated baseline)
rows.note: The caption says the additional examples support a statistically significant result in neural representation space; it does not give the individual cosine values.
rows.check: Measures additivity (linearity) of ViT-B/16 embeddings over N=10 examples, not overlapping storage of more features than dimensions. Correctly unlinked. The p-value is an aggregate; individual cosine values are not given beyond the two shown examples.

rows.subject: pixel space
rows.operation_detail: Compared additivity in pixel space with the calibrated baseline.

conditions.value: Further examples, N=10; image examples include generated and natural images

rows.measure: Statistical significance of additivity over the calibrated baseline
rows.baseline: Calibrated baseline: cosine similarity of the representations of just “A” and “B”
rows.note: The caption states that the result was not statistically significant in pixel space.
rows.check: Pixel-space control for r1. The subject is the input space, not a model. Correctly unlinked.

rows.subject: ViT-B/16
rows.operation_detail: Compared the representation of a pink elephant with the elephant-plus-ball-minus-pink-ball analogy vector.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity between the representation of the pink elephant and the analogy vector
rows.note: The caption describes this as demonstrating analogy making for a local example.
rows.check: A single illustrative analogy example (c.s.=0.92) with no baseline. It bears on the linear representation of concepts, not superposition per se. Correctly unlinked; it is anecdotal and could arguably be excluded as a row.
